title: The ten-day retreat, the hard days
hookLine: some days of the retreat are hard; the practice is to stay

lines: THE CAR IS IN THE LOT.
THE KNEES, THE BACK, THE SONGS.
cards: Somewhere in the middle of a ten-day retreat, a sensible plan forms in the mind. The car is in the lot. The keys are in the bag.
Nobody would really mind. The knees ache, the back aches, the breath is boring, and every old song and old argument is playing at once.
People who have sat these retreats tell stories about this moment; some can name the very day it came. Not everyone hits it on the same day, and some never hit it at all.

teach.b: First, why it gets hard. On day one, the newness carries you. A day or so later it's gone, and what's left is you, the cushion, and everything you'd usually drown out with a phone.
Further in, as the practice deepens, old feelings can rise to the surface. Teachers on these courses say this is expected, not a sign that something has gone wrong. Second, the instruction: stay.
Some retreats include sittings where students try not to move at all, not shifting the legs or opening the eyes, simply watching what comes up.
An ache rises, peaks, changes, fades. Restlessness rises and fades. Underneath is impermanence: nothing that arises stays.

Third, an old story about staying the right way. In the Numerical Discourses, a monk named Sona practices so hard, pacing in walking meditation, that his feet bleed, and he thinks of giving up and going home.
The Buddha asks him: when you played the lute, did it sound right with the strings too tight? No. Too loose?
No. Only when tuned just right. Effort, the Buddha says, is like that: neither strained nor slack.
Sona stays, and in the story he goes on to awakening.
Fourth, what staying means. Not gritting your teeth until you break; not running, and not forcing. Sit with the ache.
Breathe. Adjust the string if you need to.
Then stay a little longer than the plan in your head said you could.

how: On ten-day retreats, students are encouraged to stay through the difficult days, and some courses include sittings in which students try not to move, observing discomfort and restlessness as they arise and pass.

o: ten days of forcing yourself past every pain
a retreat you may leave the moment it gets hard
a silent retreat where the hard days teach you to stay

games.q: the hard days: tap the pairs.
p: sounds right only when tuned just right

s: a hard day on retreat means something has gone wrong
teachers on these courses say hard days are expected.
the Buddha told Sona to push even harder
he compared effort to a lute string: neither too tight nor too loose.
in the story, Sona stays and goes on to awakening
after the lute teaching, he tunes his effort and keeps practicing.

games.q: you're Sona. you've practiced so hard your feet are bleeding, and you're thinking of giving up and going home. what does the Buddha suggest?
o: go home; this path isn't for you.
push even harder until it breaks through.
tune your effort like a lute string, and stay.
games.why: a lute sounds right only when the strings are neither too tight nor too loose. Sona tunes his effort, stays, and in the story reaches awakening.

practice: Settle in and breathe, and when something wants your attention, an itch, a stiff shoulder, the urge to check the time, stay with it a few breaths and notice where it is and whether it changes.
If it's real or sharp pain, move gently; that's tuning the string, not failing. If it's only restlessness, see whether you can stay one breath longer than you wanted.

wordCard.voice: The ten-day retreat. On the hard days, the practice is simply to stay, with effort tuned like a lute string, neither too tight nor too loose. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali viriya: effort, energy, the steady strength the Buddha compares to a well-tuned string.

carryVoice: Your line: stay. Not too tight, not too loose. See you tomorrow.
